As we have explained, and as al-Ghazali’s words show, this unity includes multiplicity. It is a unity that gathers many things together. When we consider existence as existence—the all-embracing reality of what exists—we are looking at the level called Unity (wahidiyya). When we consider pure existence, with no other meaning or determination in its essence, we are looking at the level of Oneness (ahadiyya).
Chapter 28 — How Existence Flows Through Particular Beings

Know that beings exist in three different ways. The first is pure existence: it does not depend on anything else and is not limited by any condition. The mystics call it the hidden reality, the absolute unseen, or the divine essence in its oneness. It has no name or attribute, and we cannot grasp or know it directly. Anything that can be named or described is a concept in the mind or imagination. Anything we know is connected to something else. But this reality comes before all things and remains as it is, without change or transition. It is utterly unseen and unknown except through its effects.

In itself, God’s holy essence is neither restricted by a particular feature nor “absolute” in the sense of being conditioned by limits and distinguishing marks. The things that belong to His essence are conditions for how He appears, not causes of His existence. To say otherwise would imply some lack in Him. Here, “absolute” means that every description, rule, and attribute is denied of the innermost essence. It is not limited or changed by any name, quality, or determination. Even these denials are ideas formed by the mind, so the essence is not bounded by them either.

The second way beings exist is through something else. Their existence is limited by an added quality and described by specific features. This includes intellects, souls, the spheres, the elements, and all the beings made from them: people, animals, plants, and lifeless things.

The third is all-pervading existence. It is “universal” in a different sense from a general idea. Existence is fully real and actual, while a general idea—whether it is a natural kind or a mental concept—is vague and needs something added to make it concrete. The oneness of this existence is not numerical unity, the one from which numbers are formed. It is a reality spread through the forms of possible beings and their essences. It does not fit within any one category or limit: timeless or newly originated, prior or later, perfect or deficient, cause or effect, substance or accident, separate from matter or embodied.

In itself, it does not need anything added to it to appear in all the different levels of existence. Rather, the particular realities of the world flow from its levels and ways of unfolding. It is the root of the world, the source of life, the Throne of the All-Merciful, and what the mystics call “the Real through whom creation is made.” It is the Reality of realities. It is many while remaining one: as particular beings differ through their essences, it is timeless with the timeless, changing with the changing, understood with the intellect, and sensed with the senses. For this reason, some may mistake it for a general idea. But it is not.

Words cannot fully describe how this existence spreads through essences and includes all beings. We can only use comparisons. In one respect, it is to the beings of the world as basic matter is to particular bodies; in another, it is like a general kind, such as the most general kind, in relation to the individual things and species beneath it. These comparisons bring the idea closer in some ways and lead us away from it in others.

Understand that this existence is not the familiar general idea of existence that the mind abstracts from things. That idea is a mental concept. As we have seen, it belongs to a class of ideas that the mind forms by reflecting on other concepts. Many philosophers, especially later writers, missed this distinction.

The mystics state this plainly. The careful thinker Ṣadr al-Din al-Qunawi, after describing existence in this third sense and comparing it to matter, says: “Existence is the matter of possible beings, and the readiness of each being is prepared by the wisdom of the Creator, the All-Knowing and All-Wise, in the way He knew it to be prepared.” The common feature of these beings is weakness: each is limited by possibility, distant from the fullness of existence, and caught in multiplicity. The mystic Ibn Arabi calls this existence the “Breath of the All-Merciful.”

This distinction clears up the confusion around “the Dust” and “the Phoenix.” When the mystics call the Necessary Being “Absolute Existence,” they mean existence in the first sense: pure reality with no other thing alongside it. They do not mean this third, all-pervading existence. Confusing the two has led to serious errors: unbelief, moral license, the claim that God dwells in created things, and the idea that God takes on the limited qualities of possible beings and becomes subject to defects and change. Once we distinguish the levels of existence, the pure transcendence and holiness upheld by careful philosophers and most religious scholars remain intact.
Whoever understands my words has not lost their inner sight; only a person with clear vision can understand them.

To point to these three levels and the general ideas the mind forms from each, ʿAla al-Dawla writes in his notes on The Meccan Revelations: “True existence is God; all-pervading existence is His act; and restricted existence is its effect.” By “all-pervading existence,” he does not mean the familiar abstract idea of existence, but the reality that spreads through all things. Al-Qunawi calls it “general” because this is the broadest and most obvious feature the mind grasps first, not because this name exactly describes what it is.

Al-Qunawi also says in The Key to the Unseen that the apparent existence spread through the identities of possible beings is called “general existence,” and “the manifestation that runs through the reality of possible things.” This name points to its broadest and most obvious feature, the first one the mind can grasp; it is not an exact name for what this reality is in itself. In his commentary on the opening chapter of the Qur'an, al-Qunawi points to the first level of existence as “something the mind can understand by seeing its effect, though it cannot witness its essence.” He also writes:
Gathering is a state, not an individual thing; it has power over all individual things.
Chapter 29 — What First Flows from True Existence

Once you have understood the three levels of existence, as far as you can, you can see what first flows from the Necessary Being: all-pervading existence. In His oneness, God's essence has no description beyond itself, yet it holds every quality of beauty and majesty. All-pervading existence is also called the Cloud, the all-gathering level, the Reality of Realities, and the oneness that gathers all things. It is sometimes called the level of divine unity. When we consider the Necessary Being in relation to His names in the mind and to possible beings in the world, we speak of the level of unity and the divine presence.

This flowing forth is not causation in the usual sense. Causation requires a difference between cause and effect. It applies to particular beings, each distinct in its own way and marked by its own fixed identity. But here we are speaking of unrestricted existence. Its unity is unlike the unity of one individual, a kind, or a broader class. It is what makes every kind of unity and distinction possible.

The Necessary Being, considered through the name Allah, which gathers all the divine names, is the source of all-pervading existence. This is so because of His all-gathering reality and the particular meanings contained in His beautiful names. The mystics call this name the All-Gathering First and the Leader of Leaders. Through it, God acts on particular beings, each of which is contained within all-pervading existence. This is the sense in which we can affirm a relation between God and creation.

When philosophers say that the First Intellect is the first thing to flow from God, based on the principle that “from one, only one can proceed,” they are speaking generally about distinct beings that differ in nature and effect. In that sense, the First Intellect is first among the separate beings. But when we examine it more closely, we find all-pervading existence joined with a particular nature, limitation, and possibility. At the most basic level, then, what first flows forth is all-pervading existence itself. At each level, it is joined with a particular nature and limited in a particular way.

As with the Necessary Being, whose essence is beyond description in its oneness but includes every divine name and quality in the level of unity, all-pervading existence is distinct in itself from particular natures and fixed identities. Yet at each level it is joined with a particular nature and its accompanying features. These natures are not made separately or added to existence. What is brought about is each particular level of existence itself, not the fact that it is this particular level or its union with a particular nature. The Necessary Being's oneness is the source of all-pervading existence, and the unity of His names is the source of the world, both its existence and its particular natures. Glory to the One who joined oneness to oneness and multiplicity to multiplicity. Without this, there could be no connection between what acts and what is acted upon, and no action or creation.
A Note on Upholding God's Transcendence

As we have said more than once, the word “existence” is used in different senses. In one sense, it means a thing's reality: what rules out nonexistence. Philosophers use it in this sense for God. In another sense, it means the mental idea of existing. No reasonable person treats that idea as a thing's own reality, much less as God, who is the source of all realities and beings.

This second sense is called “relative existence,” “being there,” or “existence as a statement,” as when we say, “Homer is a poet,” or “Zayd is a writer.” This kind of existence can go together with nonexistence when we speak in different respects: Zayd may be at home and not at the market. In fact, such a statement can be called nonexistent, since it has no separate existence in the world apart from the way we describe it.

Just as philosophers use “existence” in the first sense for God, many leading mystics do as well, including Ibn Arabi, Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, and the commentator on The Meccan Revelations. Ibn Arabi and his student often use “absolute existence” for all-pervading existence—the shadow, the Cloud, or the all-gathering level—not for God as the Necessary Being. The commentator sometimes uses “absolute existence” for God. I suspect the disagreement between him and Ibn Arabi comes from using the same word in different senses.
Among those who use “existence” for God are the Persian poets Attar, Firdawsi, and Jalal al-Din Rumi. Attar writes:
The Lord whose very being is His own; all things are pages bearing signs of Him.
You are the heights and depths; I do not know what to say—whatever is, is You.
We are nothings appearing as beings; You are absolute existence; our being is yours.

Theologians who hold that God's names may be used only when scripture allows them see no doubt that “existence,” or even “the Existing,” cannot be used as a name for Him. Whether it may be used to describe Him is disputed. Some say no; others say yes, and this is the sounder view, since the word “existence,” like the word “thing,” can apply to both God and created beings, though they exist in utterly different ways. When the commentator says that God's essence is beyond existence and nonexistence, he seems to mean the abstract idea of existence, not real existence itself. He takes this to be the reason that the word should not be used for God and that those who use it are unbelievers. But this reading of the great thinkers is mistaken. All the great philosophers and mystics agree that God is beyond every defect and that His essence cannot be fully grasped. The mystics speak of a special way of knowing God: the seeker recognizes God through God when the self has fallen away in the experience of unity. Anyone who studies their books carefully will see that they do not disagree about God as the reality of existence.

The objections that the commentator raises against Ibn Arabi and his student, Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, are really about words; they agree on the main ideas. For example, Ibn Arabi says that “absolute existence” is the Real, described by every quality. The commentator objects that the Real is God, not absolute existence, whether unrestricted or restricted. But Ibn Arabi may mean all-pervading existence, which spreads through all natures and can therefore be said to bear every quality, including the qualities of created things—while God Himself remains beyond them. Or he may mean God's pure existence, in which case “every quality” means every perfection and divine quality that belongs to God Himself, not something added to His essence. It may also refer to God as He is known through the appearances of His names and qualities, which are expressions of His vast mercy, generosity, and care.

Elsewhere, Ibn Arabi writes, “In reality, there is only the Real.” The commentator replies, “Yes, but through His generosity, He has brought forth His manifestations. The outpouring has unrestricted existence, the manifestations have restricted existence, and the One who pours it forth has true existence.” Ibn Arabi also writes, “The Real is nothing but existence.” The commentator again replies, “Yes: He is true existence; His act has unrestricted existence, and its effect has restricted existence.”

After explaining that possible beings receive existence and that their natures have no existence of their own, Ibn Arabi writes, “If you understand this, you will grasp a great truth: He appears in everything, but He is not the essence of things. Glory be to Him: He is Himself, and things are themselves.” The commentator agrees: “That is right. Hold firmly to this view.” These and other objections come down to different uses of words and different ways of speaking. Words such as “essence,” “reality,” “identity,” and “self” can mean pure existence or a thing's particular nature. The same confusion arises with “existence”: it may mean God's true existence, all-pervading existence, or restricted existence. Anyone who carefully reads the commentator's notes on The Meccan Revelations will see that he and Ibn Arabi do not truly disagree about existence.

The special kind of unity taught by the mystics lies beyond what the mind can reach by reasoning alone. Until a person is guided by God, it is hard to explain in terms that fit the expectations of formal thinkers. So their words can seem to conflict. Differences of this kind appear even in scripture and the sayings of the Prophet: different religious communities appeal to the same texts while holding different beliefs. “For each of you We have appointed a law and a way.”
Shaikh Abdullah al-Ansari writes in The Stations of the Wayfarers, speaking of the unity known to a few:

The third kind of unity is God's own, which He alone deserves. He has let a glimmer of it shine into the secrets of some of His chosen ones, then left them speechless when they try to describe or explain it. The scholars of this path have tried to point toward it with elaborate names and distinctions, but words only hide it further; descriptions make it harder to approach, and explanations make it difficult to grasp. Those devoted to spiritual practice and those who experience spiritual states turn toward this unity. Reverent worshippers seek it, and those who speak of the unity that gathers all things have it in view. Yet no tongue speaks of it, and no words can point to it. True unity lies beyond anything a created being can point to.
I have answered the mystics' account of unity in these lines:

No one can make the One into one by speaking; whoever claims to describe Him has missed the point. Every description of His unity is borrowed, and the One Himself makes it fall away. His unity is His own oneness; whoever describes Him has turned away from it.
Chapter 30 — Why Possible Things Have No Existence in Themselves

From what you have heard, you may now accept the special unity of God: existence is one reality, and that reality is the Real. The natures and identities of possible beings have no real existence of their own. They appear to exist by taking on the light of existence. We understand them through the ways existence appears and unfolds. What appears in every manifestation, nature, state, and distinction is the reality of existence itself—or rather, the Real, appearing in different ways through His manifestations, names, and relations.

A particular possible nature, such as being human or being an animal, is like abstract ideas such as possibility, thingness, and nature in one respect: none has an independent existence in itself. But the difference between these two kinds lies in how we use them. When we call an existing person human, we refer to that person, whether the person exists in the world or in the mind. Words like “possibility” and “thingness,” by contrast, do not point to a separate thing in the world. In short, particular natures represent particular beings; abstract ideas describe those natures. Neither kind is a separate concrete thing that we can see or that can act on our minds and senses. Possible beings are empty in themselves. What exists always and forever is God alone. Existence is one; multiplicity and difference belong to how we know it. From one mode of existence, the mind can understand many meanings.

True existence appears to itself. This is called the Hidden of Hidden. It also appears through its act, lighting the heavens of spirits and the world of bodies. This is its manifestation as existence, called Light, through which natures and fixed identities show their features. Because these natures differ, existence appears as many in a secondary sense, though it is one in itself. Each nature becomes a mirror in which the features of the others appear, but the act of existence itself is not multiplied or repeated. The Qur'an says, “Our command is only one, like the blink of an eye.”

Multiplicity lies in the mirrors, not in the light or the act that makes it appear. The one act is a single light that reveals different natures without making them. The light of the sun seems to multiply as it shines through many windows, though the light itself is one. This, the mystics say, is why possible natures have no existence in themselves. They are not “nothing” in the sense of being just a negative idea in the mind, or merely an idea formed by thinking about other ideas. They have no existence of their own in the world. What is not existence, or something that exists in itself, cannot be made real by something else. Only existence and its different forms are real. Natures seem to exist because the mind connects them with the levels and forms of existence.

So possible natures remain without independent existence forever. They do not receive existence as a quality added to them. Instead, they become mirrors through which true existence appears, as different levels of existence take on different forms. As the poet says:
Existence flows through all things in its fullness; its distinct forms are matters of thought.
The possible’s face is dark in both worlds; its poverty never leaves it—God knows best.
The great thinkers have made this point plainly. In explaining the verse “Everything perishes except His Face,” Abu Hamid al-Ghazali describes those who know through direct experience:

They saw directly that nothing exists but God, and that everything perishes except His Face. They did not mean that things will perish at some future time. Each thing is already perishing, from beginning to end. Considered in itself, every thing is pure nothing. Considered in the way existence flows to it from the First Reality, it exists—not in itself, but in the way it turns toward its Maker. Each thing has two faces: one toward itself and one toward its Lord. From the first, it is nothing; from the second, it exists. So nothing exists but God, and everything perishes except His Face, forever.

The books of Ibn Arabi and his student, Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, are full of this teaching. They say that when they compared what they had seen directly with the Qur'an and the Prophet’s sayings, they found that it matched the plain meaning of those texts without needing reinterpretation. They therefore rejected readings by theologians and other scholars that conflicted with what they had repeatedly seen for themselves. They took the verses and sayings in their first, apparent sense, while avoiding any bodily meaning or resemblance to created things in speaking of God and His attributes.

One scholar says that religious reports should be accepted as they are, without reinterpretation or denial. By “reinterpretation,” he means giving a statement a meaning other than its usual one; by “denial,” he means refusing to accept that usual meaning. A Persian verse puts the problem this way:
To speak of Him risks likening Him to creation; to keep silent is to deny Him.

Some scholars have even condemned those who interpret verses and reports. Most religious scholars, however, hold that their apparent meanings are true, even if they also have other, deeper meanings. The Prophet is reported to have said that the Qur'an has an outer meaning, an inner meaning, a limit, and a point where it opens up. If these verses and reports did not carry their first, apparent meanings, they would be of no use to ordinary people. Instead, they would only confuse them. People understand the unclear passages in three different ways.

The first group are those firmly grounded in knowledge. They accept the first meaning without drawing from it anything that would make God deficient or contradict what is known about Him. The second group are scholars who rely on rational argument, including Islamic philosophers. They interpret the verses and reports to fit their theories, because their thinking has not moved beyond formal reasoning. The third group are strict literalists, including some Hanbali scholars and people who focus on language and reports. They remain within the bounds of the physical world and conclude that God is a body or something bodily. God is far above what they say.

For most people, especially those who study only the practical rules of religion, the third approach may seem the most suitable. Al-Ghazali says as much in The Jewels of the Qur'an: “Either be completely literal or completely transcendent and holy—as the saying goes, ‘Be wholly Jewish, or do not play with the Torah.’” But most people cannot hold to pure transcendence, so they are left with the literal approach.

The truth is that both extremes—the literalist’s and the interpreter’s—depart from the balanced path of those firmly grounded in knowledge. Each looks at the manifestations of existence with only one eye. The literalist looks with the left; the interpreter with the right. The complete knower sees with both. Every possible being has two sides: one turned toward itself and one toward its Lord. With the right eye, the knower sees God as the source of existence, appearing in every thing. All goodness, completeness, and beauty return to Him. With the left eye, the knower sees creation: it has no power except what God gives it, and can only receive His gifts. In itself, it has no existence and is marked by weakness and lack. Every flaw, loss, and failure belongs to this side.
The glass grew thin, and the wine grew thin; they seemed alike, and the matter became unclear. It was as if there were wine but no cup, and as if there were a cup but no wine.

Some ignorant imitators of the mystics have taken this too far. They lack the learning and insight of the great mystics, and their weak understanding and wavering beliefs have led them to think that the One, beyond all forms and appearances, does not truly exist. They think only the world of forms and its spiritual and physical powers are real, and that God is simply this whole visible world. They call this world the “Great Human” or the “Clear Book,” and say that each individual human being is a small copy of it. This is open unbelief and false teaching. No one with even a little knowledge would say this. To attribute it to the great mystics is a blatant lie; their deepest teachings reject it.

The confusion may come from the many ways the word “existence” is used. Sometimes it means God; sometimes it means all-pervading existence; sometimes it means the general idea of existence in the mind. The mystics often use “existence” for the shadow-like existence of particular beings, and then speak of it in ways that can sound as if they are speaking of God Himself. For example, Ibn Arabi says that whatever enters existence is limited. Al-Qunawi speaks of a hidden reality beyond the circle of existence and creation. In one of his letters, Ala al-Dawla says that above nature lies a world of absolute nonexistence, and that the darkness of nonexistence surrounds created existence, though the source of life is found within it. Elsewhere he says that above the world of life is the world of existence, and above that is the realm of the Beloved King, with no end to His realm.

In such statements, “nonexistence” may mean what is beyond this shadow-like, created existence. The word may also mean what cannot be known or described by the mind. The pure oneness of God lies beyond anything a created mind can see or grasp. “Existence” can also mean what is found or encountered. In that sense, God cannot be found as an object apart from His manifestations, even though He exists fully and in Himself. His essence appears to itself in pure oneness, the “Hidden Treasure” mentioned in a well-known saying. Then He appears in another way, through His acts and in the world. This further appearance unfolds through the forms in which He is known.

Through this later appearance, God's enduring reality is seen in the mirrors of intellect and soul, according to each observer's ability. It appears with greater or lesser clarity, depending on the level of existence and the strength of the observer's understanding. This variety of appearances does not divide God's essence, lessen its perfection, or change His eternal existence. He remains as He always was, even when nothing else existed. That is why the poet says:
The face is one, though it seems to multiply when you count the mirrors.
Chapter 31 — Why Evil Does Not Belong to Existence Itself

Know that a possible thing can be called a “thing” in two senses. One is its existence: it appears at some level, in some world. The other is its nature—what it is—which the mystics call its fixedness. This second kind of thinghood means that the mind knows a nature through the light of existence. The mind draws the nature from existence and understands it as belonging to that existence. This is true whether we mean a thing in the world or in the mind. The nature is not made or caused separately, and it is never detached from existence. This is not what the Muʿtazilite theologians mean when they speak of fixed essences.

The more careful view is that a nature is not a quality added to existence. Rather, the mind understands it through existence, and the two belong together in the thing itself. We see existence; we understand a thing's nature. This kind of “thinghood” lets us distinguish a possible nature from an impossible one. The possible nature can receive God's gift of existence and hear the command “Be,” entering the world by God's permission.
Someone might object: “You have said that each possible nature is identical with its existence in the world, and follows it. How, then, can the nature come first and receive existence?”

We answer: it does not come first in the world. But the particular forms of existence have an earlier, undivided level. This level comes from God's knowledge of Himself and of the levels of His names and qualities. Before these forms descend, divide, and become many, their names and qualities are present within God's oneness. From them come the natures and fixed identities of possible beings. These natures follow the existences God knows, because His knowledge of them is perfect and is one with His essence.

God's eternal knowledge of these natures is what allows their existences to appear later, each at its proper level. When existence flows from God and becomes distinct in the world, each form is joined to a nature. No separate act of creation is needed. So no nature comes before its existence in the world.

In God's knowledge, too, the fixed identities follow His existence, which is His knowledge of things. He knows their existences together in one simple awareness, yet knows their natures in detail. To know the complete cause is to know its effects. The same is true in the world: what flows from God and is made is the many forms of existence. Natures follow them only in a secondary sense. So when mystics say that fixed identities exist and receive God's gift of existence, they mean that each one's features appear in the light of existence. They do not mean that existence becomes a quality attached to it.

As for the verse, “Was there not a time when the human being was not even mentioned?”, the “not a thing” refers to a particular human existence, not to the human nature. The same is true of the saying, “God was, and there was nothing with Him.” For the mystics, possible natures are “things” only in the sense that they are known to God, not because they have their own existence. That is why Abu al-Qasim al-Junayd, when he heard this saying, replied, “And now it is as it was.” ʿAla al-Dawla makes the same point about those who reach unity without believing that God enters or joins created things: they see their Lord as He was when nothing was with Him, and know that He is now as He was. This is the state of unity.

Once these points are clear, we can say that natures and fixed identities do not exist on their own. First, they are gathered within unity; later, they appear among the many forms of existence. Yet when the mind considers them in themselves, apart from existence, they become the source of many judgments: possibility, limitation, and other defects. Evils and hardships that belong to these natures come from them, without being separately created. In this sense, they shield God from having defects attributed to Him.
But to ignore natures altogether leads to confusion, unbelief, and the denial of wisdom and religious law. Recognizing the way natures have their own features helps answer many difficult questions.

These questions include why evil occurs in the world and why some people sin. Such things arise from the limitations of a being’s nature, defects within it, or its lack of readiness. Here lies the secret of destiny. Some knowers of God count the fixed identities among His hidden aspects: they are forms of His self-knowledge, known before they appear. But this subject can confuse weak minds.

Few scholars can consider it without being harmed or led astray. A person needs firm knowledge, strong spiritual practice, and a steady mind to stay on the right path. Al-Qunawi says that these hidden aspects also belong to what is contained in God's oneness, but that the complete knowers understand the difference. There are deep waters here with no shore.

Al-Qunawi also says that existence appears in two ways. In one, the features of things appear everywhere; in the other, existence itself appears in each level. These are not the same: existence takes on a different form at each level, and what belongs to a thing at one level may differ from what belongs to it at another. Whether a feature is present or absent depends on its conditions. These may be a level, a state, a place, a time, or something else. The details of how existence appears are endless, even if the basic patterns are limited.
Chapter 32 — How Evil and Suffering Can Arise Without Undermining the Goodness of Existence

From what we have said, you may have understood this: when the one, true existence appears in one of the many natures—each different in meaning, in what makes it a thing, and in its implications—it casts truth upon what is false and makes that nature real through His existence. It appears in each nature according to what that nature can receive, taking on its color and a particular quality at each level where it appears.

You have already learned that these essential qualities, which philosophers call natures and mystics call fixed identities, come before particular existences in the mind but follow them in the world. What is given and brought into being is existence, not nature. So the differences among natures in themselves correspond to differences among existences in strength and weakness, priority and lateness, height and lowliness. In short, the one reality of existence appears in each thing according to what it can receive. It is like the same water in different places: here fresh and sweet, there salty and bitter. Or like sunlight, which takes on the color of the glass it passes through, though it has no color in itself.

Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Qūnawī says in a treatise on some sayings: “Whatever is, in itself, free of different limiting qualities and perfectly subtle, appears and takes a distinct form in each being, level, and world according to that being’s capacity to receive it and the way that level calls for it.”

This shows that every action or quality ascribed to a manifestation belongs to it in one respect and is denied of it in another. Each particular being has a nature and an existence, a way of being what it is and a way of appearing. God gives existence to natures; praise and thanks are His for giving goodness to things.

Every possible being has two aspects: its nature and its existence, its own possibility and its necessity through another. What we affirm of it or deny of it is true under one aspect or the other. You also know that what beings share, and what makes them good, is existence; what sets them apart and accounts for evil is their natures. So the language of declaring God beyond all likeness and describing Him in terms that apply to creatures—in God's words and in the words of His prophets—refers to these two aspects. Both are to be understood in their plain sense, without contradiction or reinterpretation.

Creation, giving, action, actuality, completion, formation, lasting existence, gentleness, and mercy come from God and His power. The capacity to receive, limitation, defect, weakness, passing away, decay, change, loss, overpowering, and anger come from creatures and from what they can receive. A Persian poet put it this way:
From that side come creation and completion; from this side, change at every moment.

Differences among the things that can receive existence, among possible realities, and among natures arise partly from their own character and partly from the most holy outpouring, called the eternal divine decree. This decree is the way things are present in God's knowledge in the best and most fitting order, following His names and qualities, which are one with His essence. Their existence in the world comes when God gives them existence at their appointed times and according to their readiness. This is called the holy outpouring and is the decree as it takes effect in the world. The measure follows God's knowledge, and neither decree is separate from His essence.

This does not mean that things do not come into being, change, or pass away, one after another. We will discuss this when we explain time, the timeless order, and eternity, and how these are ascribed to the Originator of all in a way that involves no change in His essence, qualities, or actions as His actions. When we explain how He encompasses things in time and space in a transcendent, all-embracing way, it will become clear how God speaks with His angels and messengers—not in the way the Ashʿarites say.

To sum up, the limits and defects found in the existence of possible beings come from what receives existence, not from existence itself. This answers the dualists’ objections and removes the apparent contradiction between two verses of God's Book. One says, “Whatever good comes to you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.” The other says, “Say: All is from God.” How fitting that the verse goes on to ask, “What is the matter with these people? They can hardly understand what they are told!” This points to how subtle the issue is. The question of cause and effect has confused people because it is so difficult and deep: effects are veils over the faces of their causes. Many have gone astray over it. Scholars remain puzzled; some affirm causes, while others deny them. That is why it is said that people are either puzzled or ignorant about this question. Whoever finds a way through this grave difficulty, a slippery path from which only those purified by God can escape, becomes a true believer in God's oneness without denying the causes they see.

To sum up: as we have said, every thing has a particular face turned toward the Lord of Lords, the cause of causes. Through it, the thing praises Him and declares Him free of imperfection. The power we see at work in created causes comes from one of God's beautiful names, of which that cause is a manifestation. The cause praises God through that name, in the language of its own state—not through its created self, which passes away. In one respect, differences among beings reflect differences among God's names. But evils and defects come from what each thing can receive and from its readiness, as things meet and collide at lower levels while existence descends.

All true religions teach that every good, perfection, and state of well-being comes from God, while every evil, affliction, and limitation, from whatever point of view, comes from creation. As Abraham—peace be upon him and our Prophet—said, “When I am ill, He heals me.” He attributed the illness to himself and the healing to his Lord.

God's words also point to this: “If You punish them, they are Your servants; if You forgive them, You are the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.” The punishment of ignorant, wretched souls does not come from the First Reality as an act of revenge. It follows from their own deeds and actions and from their bad character. Because of an earlier sin, they are like someone who gives in to an appetite until he falls seriously ill: on the Day of Resurrection, they themselves carry the fuel for their fire. Forgiveness and joy, by contrast, follow from the First Existence, His mercy, and the existence He gives things according to what they can receive.

In a prayer, our master Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, says that all good is in God's hands, while evil is not attributed to Him. In another saying, he says, “Whoever finds good should praise God; whoever finds otherwise should blame no one but himself.”

It is clear, then, that God gives existence, brings natures from nonexistence into being, and carries them from potentiality to actuality, from incompletion to completion, and from hiddenness to appearance. May God guide us on the straight path.
Chapter 33 — How Possible Beings Reflect the Presence of God

As we said earlier, all natures and possible beings—things that depend on God for their existence—are mirrors in which God's existence appears, and places where His sacred reality is revealed. A mirror, simply as a mirror, reflects the image that appears in it. But things we can sense have many layers and limits. They can reflect the First Reality only from a great distance, as Aristotle says in The Theology of Aristotle, also known as On Divine Lordship.

Here is the point: God reveals Himself to things in one way and appears in all possible beings in one way. This appearance in things is itself God's second appearance to Himself, at the level of His acts. His perfection is so complete that His essence overflows from itself and flows outward. This second appearance to Himself cannot be like the first. Two identical things cannot exist, and what follows cannot equal what comes before it in the fullness of existence. A ray, for example, is not as bright as the light that shines it.

People use different terms for this second appearance: the descent of God's necessary existence, or its outpouring; the Breath of the Most Merciful in one way of speaking; cause and effect in another; God's active love among people of spiritual insight; or God revealing Himself to something other than Himself. The variety of ways He appears reflects the many names and qualities in His simple, undivided knowledge. The one divine essence, whose existence depends on nothing, appears in each mirror of nature according to what that nature can receive. It does not have many kinds of appearance in itself, as some have thought. That would break God's true unity—far above Him is that.

In Chapter 63 of The Meccan Revelations, Ibn Arabi writes: “When someone sees their image in a mirror, they know for certain that they have seen it in one sense and have not seen it in another. The image may look very small because the mirror is small, or very large because it is large. They cannot deny that they saw their image. Yet they know that their image is neither inside the mirror nor between them and it. So they are neither wholly right nor wholly wrong when they say, ‘I saw my image’ or ‘I did not see my image.’ What is this image they see? Where is it? What is it like? It is absent and present, there and not there, known and unknown.

“God showed His servant this example so that they would understand: if a person is confused and unable to grasp the nature of this image—although the image itself belongs to the created world and they cannot grasp its true nature—how much more confused and ignorant must they be about the One who created it.”
